newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Occidental gains exploration rights in Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Occidental gains exploration rights in Colombia.

text.p: Occidental Petroleum Corp has won a dispute with a small indigenous community in northeast Colombia that had sought to prevent the multinational from exploring its potentially oil-rich land for crude, authorities said on Wednesday.

Mines and Energy Minister Rodrigo Villamizar said the Council of State, a body set up to resolve conflicts between Colombian citizens and the state, had overturned a high court ruling last month preventing Occidental from exploring lands long considered the property of U'wa Indians.

The previous ruling, handed down by the Constitutional Court on Feb. 3, was based on a finding that the government and Occidental had failed to ask the U'was for permission to explore their land. But the Council of State ruled by 14 to 7 that they had.

The ruling effectively cleared the way for Occidental to forge ahead with exploration activity, under an association contract with Colombia's state oil company Ecopetrol, in an area that Occidental sees as among the most promising it has access to anywhere in the world.

Villamizar told national radio that exploration activity would remain on hold, however, pending a new round of talks between government officials, representatives of Occidental and leaders of the U'wa community.

Representatives of the U'was, who number no more than about 4,000 people nationwide, had threatened at a news conference in Bogota in late January to commit mass suicide if their lands were opened up to Occidental.

Robert Stewart, corporate affairs manager for Occidental's Colombian subsidiary, Occidental de Colombia Inc., said the company had still not seen the text of the Council of State ruling. He stressed that Occidental was still open to "free and constructive dialogue" with U'wa leaders, however.
"We think it's possible for exploration activity and the preservation of the cultural integrity of indigenous communities to co-exist," he told Reuters.
He added that the sprawling Samore block affected by the Council of State ruling represented "one of the most interesting prospects" Occidental has anywhere today.

"I don't want to speculate," said Stewart, who noted that only 50 percent of the block had been explored so far. "But I can tell you that we have great expectations ... It could be in line with Cano Limon or with Cusiana," he said, referring to Colombia's two biggest oil discoveries to date.

Twenty percent of the Samore block, which Stewart described as spilling across more than 516,000 acres (209,000 hectares) in three provinces of northeast Colombia, is comprised of land belonging to the U'was.
Stewart said another 30 percent of the block was covered by national parks and was currently off limits to oil exploration or drilling.
